turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr Naidoo, come through. Your repeat-script folder is on the desk, and the pharmacy technician is sitting in so we can check the list against what you actually take.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I must apologise for being a few minutes late; the robot by the mall was backed up right down the road.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Those robots have been a nightmare all week. Nothing lost. How has the right knee been?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It has been rather troublesome, I'm afraid. The pain is there most days, particularly when I walk down to the shop.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has this worse spell been going on?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The arthritis itself is years old, but this flare... um, about six weeks. Maybe a little longer. I was going to mention the—
[SEG0007] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Sorry to cut in. Shall I open the repeat list? The computer has been dragging since the load shedding last night.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Please, go ahead. Mr Naidoo, you were on the six weeks.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. About six weeks of it being properly worse. The paracetamol takes the edge off if I sit down, but it doesn't really settle the pain.
[SEG0010] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does the knee swell?
[SEG0011] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): List is up. Paracetamol, naproxen, and omeprazole are the current repeats.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): It does swell a little, yes, mostly by supper time. Not enormous, but I notice the difference.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fever with this, or redness you've seen at home?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever at all, Doctor. I haven't seen any redness either.
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): I do apologise, I trailed off earlier. What I wished to ask is whether a stronger pain tablet might be added. My neighbour manages very well on tramadol.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll come to that. First, the paracetamol — still taking it by mouth?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. One gram, three times a day. Two of the five-hundred-milligram tablets each dose, for the knee.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): And the naproxen — what do you actually take?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): Five hundred milligrams in the morning and five hundred at night, for the knee, with food. That is what I have been doing.
[SEG0020] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): That's not what I have here. The pharmacy list says naproxen two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day. That's the strength on the last script.

[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me summarise. You believe it is five hundred milligrams twice a day, and the record says two hundred and fifty twice a day. I am not going to guess which is correct today.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I see. I may have been splitting the tablets wrongly. I would not wish to mislead you.
[SEG0023] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I can pull the original script from the batch file, but it isn't in the room.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): Do that once we're finished, please. We won't alter the naproxen strength on today's script.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The omeprazole I take at night — forgive me, that is not right. It is in the morning, twenty milligrams.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's for the stomach, while you are on the anti-inflammatory. Any burning, or black stools?
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No burning, Doctor, and the stools have been quite normal.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines, or to anything else?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): None that I know of. I have been fortunate there.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back to the stronger tablet. You are asking for tramadol?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, if you thought it appropriate. Something a little stronger. I don't sleep well when the knee throbs at night, and I—
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, I'll stop you there. The sleeping is because of the pain?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I wake once or twice, and then I lie awake a while. It isn't every night.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I understand. I am not going to add tramadol. It can make you drowsy and unsteady, and a fall would be a poor exchange.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): I quite understand. My wife would not be pleased if I took a tumble in the passage.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sensible. I also will not increase the naproxen. Have you had the kidney bloods checked?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, last year at the provincial hospital. They said it was borderline. They never gave me a number, and I couldn't tell you the month.
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): So, borderline, no figure, and the month is unclear. I won't treat that as a precise result. It is reason enough not to increase an anti-inflammatory.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you for putting it so carefully. The letter is in my other jacket at home, I'm afraid. Useless to you there.
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): No matter. Let me look at the right knee — there is no redness, it is slightly warm compared with the left, you bend it to about ninety degrees, and it feels stable.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): It catches a little at that point. I hope I am not making a fuss over nothing.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): You are not. My impression is a flare of the osteoarthritis in the right knee, not a new injury. That is provisional, from what you've told me and from the examination.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I have had the osteoarthritis for about eight years, since I retired from the post office. Walking to the shop is really my only exercise these days.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain, or shortness of breath on that walk?
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): No, neither. The knee slows me, not the chest. I did stop to chat to a neighbour about the rugby, but that is hardly medical.
[SEG0046] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Doctor, shall I mark paracetamol and omeprazole for reissue, and hold the naproxen?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. Reissue paracetamol one gram three times a day by mouth, and omeprazole twenty milligrams every morning by mouth. Leave the naproxen off until the old script is found.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems entirely fair. Should I carry on with the naproxen I have at home, or stop it?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Don't increase it, and don't assume five hundred. Until we clarify, take no more than the two hundred and fifty milligrams twice a day on the pharmacy list, with food.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Very well. I shall follow that exactly.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol regular, and rest the leg when it swells. If it has not eased in six weeks, come back and we will rethink.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it becomes much worse before then, or I cannot put weight on it?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then don't wait. Come back sooner, or go to casualty if you truly cannot walk.
[SEG0054] person_3 (CLINICAL_STAFF): I'll print the paracetamol and the omeprazole for the hatch, and I'll chase that old naproxen script this afternoon.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): One more thing. We might repeat the kidney blood test if the old result never turns up. Not today.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I would be quite happy with that. Thank you for your patience, Doctor, and my thanks to you as well.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pleasure. Mind the passage on the way out; the tiles are a bit uneven.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.

interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

omissions.text: Naproxen dose details were incompletely recorded: the patient said he had been taking 500 mg in the morning and 500 mg at night with food, while the pharmacy list said 250 mg twice a day; the medication entry lacks the conflicting dose values and route.
The previous kidney blood test was done last year at the provincial hospital and the patient was told it was 'borderline'; the month and numeric result were unknown.
The doctor explicitly said he would not increase the naproxen because of the borderline prior kidney result.
The patient asked whether he should continue the naproxen he already had at home or stop it; this specific question is not recorded.
The follow-up safety advice included 'come back sooner' if much worse before six weeks, in addition to going to casualty if truly unable to walk.
